What’s in My Pack…

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s raingear, gloves, hat, a blanket, sweatshirt, a calculus book, some water….
  • I also have my astronomy and chemistry books in there.
  • I don’t expect to be calculating any derivatives out on the trail, though I suppose there could be some deep analysis on rates of change over time, especially involving hiking distances per day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well, let’s see. There’s raingear, gloves, hat, a blanket, sweatshirt, a calculus book, some water….

In a recent development, hold up. What was that? A calculus book?

Yes. I also have my astronomy and chemistry books in there. Back when I was in college – before the internet but after color TV was apparently invented – our college professors assured us we would all be using calculus in our engineering careers. I’ve wondered for decades when I would ever use this… material (putting it politely), other than to teach it to my son or other engineering students who struggled with higher-level math. So, after thirty-five years, I’ve finally found a use for it.

I don’t expect to be calculating any derivatives out on the trail, though I suppose there could be some deep analysis on rates of change over time, especially involving hiking distances per day.

For astronomy, I love looking at the stars. Sure, it’s engineering astronomy with lots of galactic calculations for weights, trajectories and distances, but it has a few very pretty star charts that would look great at night. Not so much at 10 a.m. on a random Saturday, but considering Michigan, the probability of unusual weather events is never zero.

What about chemistry? Its really more of a canary in a coal mine for me… or more accurately, a canary in my backpack. The only chemical reaction I’m investigating is whether the chemistry book turns out wet and its pages become more pulp-like, in which case I’ve learned something.

My pack liner is no longer waterproof.

In a recent development, I’d take my statistics book, which is a heavier, but I actually like that one. Yes, I know. I have a bit of a twisted mind to enjoy statistics. The other choice was my Engineering Project Management book. While hiking the AT is, in itself, an entire project management adventure, and I suspect Change Control may be a solid fireside topic while hiking, I still need that book for work-related activities.

A better question may be WHY do I have these three books in my pack?

It has been revealed that weight. They help my pack get up to 30 pounds, which I hope is my peak hiking weight when I’m on the trail next March. The calculus book is a whomping 5 pound and a touch over 15 ounces. Lots of “good times” in that book. Chemistry is another five pounds and almost 2 ounces while astronomy is in between with 5 pounds and 5 ounces.

Perhaps a better title for this post would be “How Am I Preparing for My AT Hike?” In which case, those books are involved, but no, they aren’t going on the trail with me in four months.

For preparing my body for the trail, there are three strategies I’m using:.

Southeastern Michigan doesn’t have mountains, and the hills are more bump-like, but they are there. Tossing a 30-pound pack on my back and hiking 5–6 miles is a decent warm-up. I’m trying to do that every week.

In a recent development, right now, I just finished a five-day continuous stretch of doing this every morning, as I had some vacation time still to burn from work. I’m assessing how my body handles it, what that strange feeling is in my legs, why my ankles are sore, and trying to force myself to get up, out of a comfortable bed, and hike in sub-30-degree weather. It’s been challenging but so far, OK. I am glad, though, to take a break over the next few days and instead keep working on the other two strategies.

Besides just working on my body, I’m also testing how various software works while on day hikes – my Garmin In-Reach Mini has passed my previous checks and now has its subscription suspended for another few months until I really need it, but testing Day One (a journaling app), Grammarly (to well… help with my grammar) and hopefully, WordPress to see how a post or two work here when I’m coming off a hike when I tired, hungry and just want to start my drive home with the heat on full blast.

What would be considered the easiest is actually one of the harder ones for me. A good workout at the gym is two hours. That’s enough time to get at least three miles on the treadmill (at 3.4 mph with a 6–7° uphill grade), core work, strength training, stretching and maybe finishing by laying on a hydro lounger at the end.

According to recent reports, sadly, my job takes up longer hours than I want to admit at times, but at least I enjoy doing what I am doing at the office as well as the people I work with. The problem comes at the end of the day. If I don’t leave early enough, I don’t get to the gym until after 5 p.m., in which case it’s impossible to get a decent work out and get home in time to cook dinner for my wife. I’m left wondering where the day went.

Sources indicate that yes, it’s true I could get up earlier in the morning, but… that isn’t happening. Probably won’t happen on the trail either, to be fair. Getting up before the sun rises is something I consider a necessary evil to continue getting a paycheck. Getting up even earlier to willingly work out is far worse and would fall into the category of a malicious act of cruelty to my body.

This is strangely enough, the easiest and most satisfying. I’m doing a routine of about thirty minutes with ankle strengthening, core work and stretching. It’s something casual to do while watching TV and the time just passes. It’s not the most useful, but hopefully it will help prevent something like an ankle sprain.

As for my actual gear list. Yes, I’ll post it. It will probably be right after the Christmas holidays, as I have some fresh gear that absolutely needs to be weighed, manhandled and experimented with. My hope is less than 20 pounds base weight for starting in March, with a fully loaded pack of under 30 pounds. Whether I hit that target or not, is in jeopardy with the requirement of a bear can, but that’s another discussion….

About me? Sure. I’m a native Detroiter and have lived my whole life in Michigan where I live with my wife – more than 25 years – and a couple of college-aged children. Well, technically the kids live off at college but they do come home to make the house look a natural disaster struck while we weren’t looking. I’m an engineer, working for one of the Big Three automakers and have well over 30 years of experience doing everything from breaking transmissions to quality improvements and even designing cooling systems for both trucks and cars. Outside of work, I love exploring and spending time outdoors. I’ve learned a lot about camping over the last few decades, including relearning wonderful lessons like not leaving an unlocked cooler in camp and proper flow directions on my water filter. Somewhere in there, I fell in love with backpacking and found a whole new world of mistakes I can learn from. Eventually, I discovered long-distance thru-hiking and convinced both my job and my family that taking a vacation from me for six months would be beneficial to them (suckers!). Catch me on a good day, and I’d be happy to talk about camping, backpacking, video games, books, music or just about anything else fun. Just don’t ask me about spreadsheets, checklists, FMEAs or change control meetings.

I thought the books were reading material while you wait for rescue after breaking your ankle after falling down a ravine… ;-P No – wait, if I were stuck reading calculus I’d just want to end it right then and there….

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

Industry observers note that the Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

In a recent development, according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

In a recent development, the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

“He was really lucky,” said Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

By the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

Sources indicate that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

According to recent reports, the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Recent findings suggest that ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed blueprint.

In a recent development, despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

Keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

According to recent reports, at the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we both thought the place we slept in last night was haunted. It was on the backside of a thousand-year-old church, with one wall actually serving as the back of the altar. We both woke up in the middle of the night feeling really hot and smelling a sewer odor. Knockerz had some strange dreams, as did I.

Recent findings suggest that when we left, my phone died as I tried to disconnect from the Wi-Fi. After a restart, Knockerz’s phone suddenly started talking to her—something it never does.

We headed out around 7:00 AM while it was still in the high 50s. We also lost an hour crossing the water: Spain keeps the same time all the way out, but when you drop into Portugal, the clocks go back an hour. A high-speed train barreled by shortly after we set off.

We’ve been navigating our own Camino route choices since entering Portugal, generally following the official routes. This has allowed us to get off the beaten path, explore the backcountry, and see areas untouched by millions of pilgrims over the centuries. Of course, self-made routes sometimes come with obstacles, like busy highways with no shoulder.

According to recent reports, at one point, I pulled up a map and realized we were on the coastal route. We’ve been bouncing between the coastal route (slightly inland and more popular) and the littoral route (which hugs the coastline and isn’t on many maps) because they run so close together.

It has been revealed that we stopped at a cafe for some caffeine and breakfast treats. The pastries here are different from Spanish treats—more layered, like a croissant, and only slightly sweet. I also noticed people saying “bom caminho” instead of the Spanish “buen camino.”.

In a recent development, the people here are very friendly, constantly greeting us with bom dia (good day). We’ve started practicing our basic Portuguese greetings:.

According to recent reports, we bumped back out to the coast where the littoral and coastal paths briefly share a path. A cool coastal fog sheltered us from the sun as the air warmed into the 60s.

Sources indicate that we enjoyed the littoral route past a wide beach featuring an old fort—its design looked remarkably similar to a fort we visited in St. Augustine, Florida. After that, we walked on a long boardwalk through a marshy area for several miles.

In a recent development, near Âncora, we took a littoral path out to the coast that forced us to walk through heavy sand dunes. It was exhausting, so we decided to bail and take an alternate route along a busy road.

After walking about a mile of cars whizzing past on a narrow sidewalk (and climbing about 500 feet off the beach), I found a quieter parallel road winding through local villages.

At this point, we were starving, so we found a restaurant that served a wonderful, incredibly cheap meal. Afterward, we made our way back to the coast to rejoin the littoral route.

In a recent development, we walked through farm fields on a narrow path paved with six-inch rocks, much like an old Roman road we traveled in Spain. Our path shifted through a mix of paved tracks, cobblestones, and large boulders. With the fog mostly burned off, the sun rays grew hot, but a constant, cold ocean breeze kept us comfortable. Most of the coastline here is rocky, dotted with tidal pools.

As we approached our final destination, we could spot a castle up on the hill and what looked like a grand structure on the same hilltop. It had been a long, 17-mile day, and we were both completely exhausted.

It has been revealed that we finally arrived in Viana do Castelo, a very cool medieval town that happened to be hosting a massive medieval (and Renaissance) festival! We wandered around for a while, taking in all the people dressed and acting like historical figures.

Recent findings suggest that tired out, we found a place to sit, enjoy some Portuguese-sized glasses of red wine, and people-watch for a couple of hours. It was actually quite cold, even in the middle of June!

Recent findings suggest that we finally headed to our room, which happened to be located in the basement. Honestly, it was perfect—we were so tired and ready for some rest. Especially Knockerz, who needed to sleep off the memory of the farting ghost hotel from the night before!

#172419. Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1689 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • It has been revealed that the journey has not gone according to plan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

It has been revealed that the journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

Sources indicate that while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

Given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid prepares. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

But this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

It has been revealed that roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

For most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

By the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and initiative ahead.

The route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

It has been revealed that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

Sources indicate that I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with fresh designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

It has been revealed that food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Sources indicate that safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

It has been revealed that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

In a recent development, we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

In a recent development, successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

Sources indicate that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

Industry observers note that I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

Sources indicate that the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

According to recent reports, the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

You can follow the expedition here.

No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (390 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • It has been revealed that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is promptly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

It has been revealed that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

It has been revealed that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

It has been revealed that once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

It has been revealed that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

Latest Update: Preparing for 2200….Because One Does Not Simply “Pop Out for a bit of a Hike”

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Preparing for a thru hike on Appalachian Trail truly begins with just one burning question;  “What will I actually need to walk 2200 miles?”   That’s pretty simple and straightforward right?
  • Suddenly, you find yourself manically comparing sleeping bags by their temperature rating, researching water filters like you’re prepping for the apocalypse, and obsessing over the ratio of weight and R-rating of every single sleeping pad in existence.
  • According to recent reports, relax……You’re definitely not the first, or the last hiker to become immersed (obsessed?) in the vortex that is thru hiking prep!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Preparing for a thru hike on Appalachian Trail truly begins with just one burning question;  “What will I actually need to walk 2200 miles?”   That’s pretty simple and straightforward right? Theoretically, yes………that is, of course, until you discover the mind-numbing multitude of content creator gear videos.

Suddenly, you find yourself manically comparing sleeping bags by their temperature rating, researching water filters like you’re prepping for the apocalypse, and obsessing over the ratio of weight and R-rating of every single sleeping pad in existence. Your hike is still months away, but you’ve already downloaded four GPS trail apps, scheduled transportation,  meticulously planned your daily mileage to the foot and plotted every daily campsite  down to the hour of  arrival.

According to recent reports, relax……You’re definitely not the first, or the last hiker to become immersed (obsessed?) in the vortex that is thru hiking prep! Perhaps I can break it down and make it a little more palatable.

Recent findings suggest that first comes the backpack. It should be light, durable, comfortable, and large enough to hold everything you need—which, according to differing opinions, is both nothing and several highly specialized pieces of equipment. First, try the pack on in the store. Bring your gear, (yes, really do this) load up the pack you’re interested in, and then look yourself wearing it the in the mirror. Pay attention at how it feels. Walk around to see how securely it sits. Then, ask yourself….do I look ready to summit a mountain or preparing to flee a small country? Adjust your choice according to what you see and feel. Lastly, never, ever choose your pack based on the popularity of it, the aesthetics, or because the unsolicited opinion of some random internet blogger.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s your shelter. You want something weatherproof, spacious, easy to set up, and light enough that you won’t begin to question your life choices by mile four. Picture this;  You finally pull the trigger on the tent;  the eager  salesperson assures you that it’s really simple to pitch. You proudly take it home and then spend twenty five minutes trying to decipher the pitching instructions, and ultimately end up with what, oddly, looks like a very expensive kite! Key advice: Research. research, research! Take your time, debate with your eager brain. and finally choose the “one” based solely on what YOUR hiking style looks like. With so many options and opinions out there, only your opinion matters!

Recent findings suggest that the art of  deciding if a sleeping bag or quilt…..down or synthetic …….or temperature rating, is for you, is another deeply personal decision. When and where are you starting? Average temperatures where you’ll be at that time of year? Lightweight or no? Inflatable pad or closed foam? Answer these questions, imagine scenarios,  and the decision will be much clearer.

Food actually takes up surprisingly little space…..that is,  until you remember you’ll need to eat it every day. Focus on a balance of carbs, protein, and pleasure.

As a novice, I bought some of those fancy dehydrated meals labeled “creamy pasta primavera,” or “Spaghetti with meat sauce”. I added the correct amount of boiling water, and soon I discovered that the words “creamy” or “meat” were undoubtedly creative writing! Still, in all fairness , it did have calories, and, in the end, calories are the fuel of the trail.

Clothing……now this decision becomes just another expedition into the unknown. Basically, you need layers for warmth, rain protection, sun protection, and the full understanding that your clothes may never again smell like laundry.

Industry observers note that I pack two shirts; one for hiking, and one for sleeping, two pair of socks, two underwear, and one pair of long pants and one pair of shorts. That’s it, because apparently I’m going into the wilderness, not to a four-day business conference.

According to recent reports, finally, you weigh your pack. You realize that it weighs enough that to suddenly start to reconsider your aims, question all of your hiking friendships, and immediately begrudge the person who told you that hiking was “just walking.” You remove a book, a camp mug, and a backup pair of pants. Then you eventually load them back because what if you want coffee while reading in clean pants? I mean….that makes sense right??

Pick the gear you bring and the total weight of the full kit solely on what you’re honestly willing to carry.

Industry observers note that the key, you’ll learn, is to pack what you need, to test it BEFORE you leave, and accept that your first massive purchase may be a tiny scale. The Appalachian Trail doesn’t care whether your gear matches. It cares if you can carry it safely, use it efficiently, and still keep walking when your feet have begun filing formal complaints !

According to recent reports, so, you now shoulder your pack, you take a few determined steps around the block, feeling great about your newfound expertise, and feel like you’re ready for anything……..but then you remember your loaded food bag is still sitting on the kitchen table. Ugh!

For reference, I have included pictures of my full gear setup in hopes it will give you some reference. GOOD LUCK!

Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (336 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • In a recent development, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

In a recent development, the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

Industry observers note that A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He noted climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

#172414. Tech Report: Bears, Moldy Gear & Navigation Mishaps: My First Solo Backpacking Adventure on the Florida Trail

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2570 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Bears, Moldy Gear & Navigation Mishaps: My First Solo Backpacking Adventure on the Florida Trail

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s something empowering about stepping into the wilderness alone, knowing that whatever happens, you’re the one who has to figure it out.
  • Recent findings suggest that for my first-ever solo backpacking trip, I set out to hike a 60 mile section of the Florida Trail through the Ocala National Forest and Juniper Wilderness Area.
  • What I didn’t anticipate was just how much the trail would throw at me in four short days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Follow Colleen Wilson and Lane Early.

There’s something empowering about stepping into the wilderness alone, knowing that whatever happens, you’re the one who has to figure it out.

Recent findings suggest that for my first-ever solo backpacking trip, I set out to hike a 60 mile section of the Florida Trail through the Ocala National Forest and Juniper Wilderness Area. I’ve spent thousands of miles backpacking alongside Lane, often leaning on his experience and confidence in the backcountry. This time, I wanted to put my own skills to the test. I wanted to see what it felt like to navigate the challenges, make the decisions, and handle whatever the trail threw at me without someone else to lean on.

What I didn’t anticipate was just how much the trail would throw at me in four short days. What started as a simple, well-planned backpacking trip, quickly turned into some of the most challenging days I’ve ever experienced on the trail and with so many things going wrong.

Between a mold-infested sleeping bag, curious black bears (including a face-to-face encounter), countless tick and chigger bites, sleepless cold nights, unexpected detours due to navigational mistakes, and a few genuinely beautiful stretches of wilderness, this trip turned into an adventure I won’t soon forget.

Recent findings suggest that more importantly, it built a confidence in myself that I hadn’t fully tapped into before. I discovered that I really enjoy the solitude, the independence, and the sense of empowerment that comes with figuring things out on my own.

Sources indicate that my dad dropped me off at Rodman Dam around 1:30 p.m., after we first cached some water at the County Road 316 crossing. I headed north through the tall longleaf pine forests, with sections of lightly overgrown trail scattered throughout the afternoon.

Industry observers note that I encountered only two northbound hikers during the first few miles, and they would turn out to be the only hikers I’d see over the entire 60-mile stretch. Within the first hour, I also came across some fresh bear scat, a friendly little reminder that I was no longer walking through the Florida I was accustomed to growing up here in the Sunshine State.

I made it about seven miles before finding a spot off-trail to set up camp around 5:30 p.m. I could hear ATVs riding throughout the area, and rather than push on toward the campground, I decided to call it a day and settle in so I could enjoy some reading in the tent before dinner.

That’s when things started getting interesting.

After setting up camp, I discovered that my sleeping bag had developed mold all over it since the last time I’d used it. Awesome.

So, I laid the bag outside on the ground beside my tent to start drying before I would pack it away in my backpack and hope it wouldn’t get cold enough that I would actually need it.

According to recent reports, after prepping dinner in my tent, which consisted of cold soaking some ramen in a talenti ice cream container, I heard sniffing around my tent. I turned around and found myself practically eye-to-eye with a black bear investigating my moldy sleeping bag.

According to recent reports, my first reaction was to yell, “Get out of here bear!” Making my voice deeper and louder with each attempt at repeating this chant. It jumped back, startled by my yelling.

It has been revealed that I grabbed my bear spray, got out of the tent, and yelled until it eventually wandered off. It kept stopping to look back at me curiously before disappearing out of sight. Not exactly the wildlife encounter I’d been hoping for on my first solo night.

I packed up my food and ate dinner a good distance away from camp, making sure to keep everything bear-proofed.

Industry observers note that naturally, I was now convinced the bear would be returning for a second visit. Like they do in every story you hear about when a person is attacked by a bear and decides to sleep with their food even after a bear sniffs their campsite the first time.

Recent findings suggest that then I discovered it wasn’t just my sleeping bag. My sleeping bag liner and pillow were all covered in mold, too. This was going to be a long first night.

At this point, I wasn’t going to be using any of this gear and all I had to rely on was my sleeping pad and a makeshift pillow made from a stuff sack and anything I could find in my pack to give it some volume. I could only hope that all the clothing layers in my pack would be enough to get me through the night as I layered them on, one-by-one.

And because apparently everything comes in threes, I found a tiny tick on my leg while changing clothes for bed.

I crawled into my tent, listened to coyotes howling in the distance, and tried to settle in with a book. Their howls seemed to get closer as the evening went on. Each sound startled me awake, thinking the bear was returning to take me out.

According to recent reports, at this point I was questioning even sticking out this backpacking trip and considering calling it quits by calling for a pickup. It was going to be a tougher few days than I’d anticipated. But, as they say, “Never quit on a bad day.” I’d try to make it through the night and assess things tomorrow.

It has been revealed that there were three main reasons. First, my sleeping setup was covered in mold, and although I initially refused to use it, I eventually got cold enough to give in. I ended up wearing practically every layer I had in my pack, including three pairs of socks, before finally pulling the moldy sleeping bag over my feet.

Second, every unfamiliar noise had me convinced a bear was circling my tent.

And third, the ATV riders and country boys in trucks seemed to be going strong until around midnight.

Needless to say, I was ready to get moving at sunrise.

It has been revealed that the morning brought some beautiful stretches of trail, although there were plenty of overgrown and thorny sections to navigate. At one point, I heard what I believe was another bear charging onto the trail behind me. I made my way swiftly toward the busy traffic of CR 316, where I felt a little more comfortable.

I accidentally walked about 0.4 miles past Store 88 where I planned to charge my phone which I needed for navigation and had to backtrack. While there, I met a 70-year-old British guy named Calvin Kline, who was working on fixing up the old place alongside his elderly dog. We chatted for about 45 minutes about life experiences and places we have traveled that we both had in common. One of those unexpected trail encounters that makes long-distance hiking so interesting.

According to recent reports, after lunch, I pushed on for another five or so miles until reaching the Salt Springs blue-blaze junction. There was a bench where I’d planned to take my dinner break, but instead I discovered something much more key: a campground another 6.5 miles ahead that had bear boxes.

I desperately needed a bear box.

It was already a little after 5 p.m., but I knew I needed to make it there. I pushed through the remaining miles and arrived shortly after 8 p.m. and hiking by headlamp.

I set up camp, secured my food in the bear box, and finally felt like I could relax a little. Dinner was cold-soaked ramen that I’d started preparing 6.4 miles earlier.

Recent findings suggest that after dinner I tried to access the food in the bear box and the doors were jammed. Great. Now I would really need to pull the plug and call for a pickup in the morning. No food means no fuel to keep hiking, unless I could find someone camping in the area that could help me get the doors unjammed. Eventually I broke into the box and was relieved that I didn’t have to quit, again.

There were other campers around, a secure place to store my food, and a much better chance of getting some sleep.

After the previous night, it felt like a luxury to not have to sleep with my food in this heavily bear dense area.

I woke up at sunrise and headed out through a beautiful prairie section before entering one of my favorite stretches of the entire trip: the Juniper Wilderness Area.

Sources indicate that the trail through the forest was absolutely gorgeous. It was one of those sections that makes you forget about all the little inconveniences of backpacking and reminds you exactly why you spend so much time out here.

Industry observers note that eventually, I made my way to Juniper Springs Recreation Area, where I had planned a seven-mile kayak float. The current was ripping pretty good and with all the down trees it made for quite the obstacle course. At one point I was pinned in between a down log and some overhanging brush and ended up snapping my sunglasses into two pieces.

A few miles into the float I met Bryan, who works for the local kayaking tech giant. We ended up floating about 3.5 miles together, chatting and swapping stories about Florida and it’s wild backcountry along the way. It was a nice change of pace from the solitude of the trail.

According to recent reports, I camped at the recreation area that evening for $50, charged my electronics, and met a couple from Ohio who work for the North Country Trail. We spent a while chatting and they were eager to ask questions about my experience on The Florida Trail so far as they were day hiking sections of it during their visit to the state.

It was a much-needed reset after two eventful days in the woods.

I woke up at sunrise with the goal of hiking the remaining miles to Alexander Springs, where my parents were scheduled to pick me up.

I believe I had around 18 miles left.

According to recent reports, the morning started off well, but somewhere around lunchtime, I managed to make a pretty significant navigation mistake. I sat down on a log to eat, got back on trail, and somehow ended up hiking in the wrong direction, back toward a road I’d already passed.

Recent findings suggest that by the time I realized what I’d done, I’d walked 1.7 miles in the wrong direction. That meant an additional 3.4 miles of bonus hiking for the day.

Sources indicate that exactly what I needed. Plus, the trail had was quite overgrown and I was covered in spiky stickers.

I picked up the pace to make sure I’d still reach my parents on time. Along the way, I continued seeing plenty of bear scat, including some that looked particularly fresh.

Then I came upon a very large black bear directly on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that I startled it, and it took off running with such incredible speed and force that, for a split second, I was terrified it was charging straight toward me. Thankfully, it veered into the woods and disappeared.

I spent the next mile or so periodically shouting, “HEY BEAR!” with my bear spray close at hand.

For the remainder of the hike, I found myself constantly scanning every turn in the trail, anticipating another bear around the next corner.

Recent findings suggest that it was an interesting balancing act. I needed to speed hike to make my scheduled pickup time, but I also didn’t want to move so swiftly as to startle another bear.

Eventually, I made it to the forest road and found a log to sit on while waiting for my parents.

I was exhausted, but incredibly proud of myself.

I had navigated the trail, dealt with unexpected challenges, made mistakes and figured them out, and pushed through situations that would have been much easier with someone else there to lean on.

According to recent reports, and honestly? I already felt ready to keep going.

But those miles would have to wait. I couldn’t stand the thought of spending another night in my moldy sleeping bag, especially without a bear canister or bear box to store my food.

Four days was enough for this adventure.

One of the things I appreciated most about this trip was how it changed my perspective on Florida.

According to recent reports, for a long time, I associated Florida with bustling cities, traffic, and endless stretches of concrete. I spent time commuting an hour to work in Miami, and my idea of escaping the city was taking a scenic backroad on a weekend drive to my home in Fort Lauderdale.

I never really appreciated just how much wilderness existed beyond the interstates connecting Florida’s major cities.

In a recent development, after walking more than 500 miles through Florida’s wilderness over the last several years, I’ve come to see the state in an entirely different light. There are enormous stretches of forests, springs, prairies, rivers, and protected wilderness that feel worlds away from the metropolitan areas most people associate with Florida.

There’s still a wild Florida out there. You just have to get off the interstate to find it.

More than anything, this trip gave me a new appreciation for what I’m capable of on my own.

I’ve spent so much of my backpacking experience alongside Lane, and while I’ve learned an incredible amount from him, I think there’s something important about stepping away from the comfort of having someone more experienced beside you.

In a recent development, you have to trust your own judgment. You have to make your own decisions. When something goes wrong, there’s nobody to immediately turn to for reassurance or a solution.

I loved the solitude. I loved making my own decisions, moving at my own pace, and having the freedom to experience the wilderness on my terms.

And perhaps most importantly, I came away with a confidence that I hadn’t realized I was missing.

Sources indicate that I don’t need to wait for someone else to be available to go backpacking. I don’t need someone else’s experience to validate my own abilities.

And I have a feeling this won’t be my last solo adventure.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a fresh attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

It has been revealed that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

Sources indicate that this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” said Kondrashkin.

Recent findings suggest that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

Sources indicate that on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#172410. Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (610 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (610 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • According to recent reports, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

According to recent reports, kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Sources indicate that neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Recent findings suggest that lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Recent findings suggest that kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch aims to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

Industry observers note that this is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Recent findings suggest that simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his intends while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

#172408. Tech Report: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1254 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • It has been revealed that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • According to recent reports, sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It indicated again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

It has been revealed that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

According to recent reports, sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Industry observers note that after 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang mentioned: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Recent findings suggest that several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

It has been revealed that “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

It has been revealed that when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

During their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s strategy to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

Sources indicate that on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

It has been revealed that “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang mentioned. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

According to recent reports, the climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

Recent findings suggest that the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

It has been revealed that the climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Sources indicate that climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

According to recent reports, rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Industry observers note that strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

It has been revealed that strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

The climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

#172406. Tech Report: Te Araroa day 32: A cruisy start to the CSQ, and LOFI is born

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1586 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Te Araroa day 32: A cruisy start to the CSQ, and LOFI is born

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1586 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 20km, Paeroa Rail Trail Motel to Daly’s Clearing hut.
  • We knew we only had a relatively short walk on this first day, and had a fairly relaxed start.
  • Industry observers note that pre CSQ selfie, leaving the motel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

20km, Paeroa Rail Trail Motel to Daly’s Clearing hut.

We knew we only had a relatively short walk on this first day, and had a fairly relaxed start. We had to walk through Paeroa and grabbed coffee on the way to the famous L&P bottle. For those not in the know, Lemon & Paeroa (L&P) is a lemonade drink ‘world famous in Latest Zealand,’ as the strapline goes.

Industry observers note that pre CSQ selfie, leaving the motel. By Sinéad, of course!

Me and Sinéad at the L&P bottle. I have funky new socks! Photo by Lindsay.

After that, we joined the Hauraki Rail Trail, a cycle path that would take us to the start of the Kaimai mountain range. The bike path was flat and easy walking, and ran next to the road to start with. It was so nice to not have to worry about the cars whizzing past! After a bit the track turned off the road and onto some farmland, and was quite scenic. Annabel was on the phone, but the rest of us walked along mostly together, having some nice chats.

Industry observers note that after a bit more farmland, we started following the Ohinemuri River as it headed into Karagahake Gorge. The river was super pretty, but soon we crossed a suspension bridge – the first of several on this trip – and turned onto another path that would lead up a tributary of the main river. I hadn’t realised but this track went through some old mining tunnels, some of which were quite long and dark! Of course we all had head torches though.

Looking up the river towards Karagahake Gorge.

Walking through the historic buildings by the river. Photo by Sinéad.

Sources indicate that what am I looking at? Photo by Sinéad.

On the Windows Walk – view from an old mining tunnel.

I guess this is one of the windows they’re talking about.

Industry observers note that out the end of the tunnels, the track continued along the river. It was beautiful, easy walking and a great way to ease back into hiking after several days off. I was already glad we came on this side quest! The river was deep and clear and looked amazing to swim in. We knew we would hit a river-side campsite at Dickey’s Flat at around lunchtime so we planned to have a dip there. But at around 11.30 we rounded a corner and saw a beautiful little waterfall with a massive pool of water in front of it. It looked too inviting and we decided to swim there and take an early lunch.

Walking along the river. Photo by Annabel.

Recent findings suggest that me and Sinéad getting in the water. Photo by Annabel.

The water was freezing! But it was very refreshing. We sat on the river bank to eat lunch and dry off. A large group of people came along to have a tea break there – they looked like a local tramping club and they were doing a loop along a different track back to Karangahake Gorge.

Recent findings suggest that from the waterfall, the track continued along the pretty river to Dickey’s Flat campsite. The river there was also nice, but not as deep or swimmable and we were glad we stopped for an early lunch. At the end of the Windows Walk through the tunnels, the DOC sign had said 4km and 2 hours to the campsite. We scoffed at that at the time, as the path was flat and easy. But after our extended lunch and swim break, it actually did take two hours. No worries, we had plenty of time that day. As we left the campsite, another sign said 3 hours to do the 8km to the hut. Again, we didn’t think it would be that long.

But as we were leaving the car park, the track took us through a field where a just-born calf was trying to stand up for the first time! We stood and watched for quite some time. There was another cow and slightly older calf in the field with them, and they were super cute too! The cows were of a type that I don’t think I’ve seen before. They looked really fluffy and the adults had a very sweet little topknot on top of their heads.

Crossing the river, in classic thru-hiker style with my towel and underwear drying on my pack. Photo by Sinéad.

The cow and slightly older calf.

Sources indicate that leaving the cows, the track became a little rougher as it followed the river. I had stuck with the others earlier in the day, but on this slightly more challenging terrain I preferred to move a little faster and pulled ahead a bit. We met up again though when I stopped for water at an accessible bit of river. Shortly afterwards, the track headed up a pretty steep hill which was a shock to the system after 3 days of no hiking and an easy morning!

Recent findings suggest that clearly the four of us have been hiking together long enough now to have developed a bit of a hive mind. When I caught up to Sinéad and Lindsay after getting water, they said they had been talking about trail names, which I had also been thinking about. Lindsay suggested LOFI for me – last out, first in – for my habit of being the last to leave in the morning and overtaking everyone else partway through the day. I like this, and I think I’ll adopt it. It’s better than Pee Sticks anyway! Annabel we thought should be Gourmet. Her food is always the fanciest trail food you ever did see. Some evidence:.

“I’ll be right there, I’m just making a bruschetta right now” – Annabel.

“Who bought sourdough? Oh it must be Annabel” – Lindsay.

Brought an avocado, pesto, cherry tomato and sundried tomato sandwich on sourdough for lunch this day.

Sinéad we agreed should be something to do with swimming. She’s such a water baby and is always the first to suggest a dip! Is there an water nymph in Irish folklore? This is a work in progress.

Lindsay we were struggling with. ‘Is it because I don’t have a distinct personality?’ No Lindsay, you are an individual and we love you very much. But she hasn’t had quite such a recurring theme throughout the hike as the rest of us. Another work in progress!

There was a bit more up and down through some pleasant forest. The bush over here is beautiful, but unfortunately I have seen it quite a lot and I don’t really appreciate it as much as I should. I’m more of a massive mountain views girl! Eventually I arrived at the junction for the hut. The sign mentioned 20 minutes but I popped out in the clearing pretty soon after. The hut looked unoccupied, and a quick peek inside confirmed I was the only one around so far. By the time the others were trickling in, I had filtered water and was waiting for my electrolytes to dissolve.

It has been revealed that clearly, I have low standards for hut cleanliness and smell because Lindsay came in and immediately opened all the windows and doors as apparently it smelled damp. I hadn’t noticed up to that point, but she was right. I had been to this hut before, and remembered that there was a fair bit of rubbish around. This was still the case, but overall the hut is in decent condition if a little tired. But it’s always a delight not to have to pitch a tent!

We made dinner, some of us with more success than others… Then Annabel was very keen that we should play a game. Someone had left Snakes and Ladders in the hut, unfortunately without a dice to use. The numbers 1-6 were written inside the lid of the box, and we ‘rolled’ by putting a Connect 4 piece inside and shaking it. After that, we were pretty tired and wanted to go to bed, but I needed to set out the route options for tomorrow. Basically, we could take an easier and more scenic, but longer route, or a shorter but muddier and less nice route. After a bit of discussion, we settled on the longer, scenic route. I thought the two might take around the same time, and sometimes that’s more important than distance. Then we finally called it a night, although twice when I was juuuust falling asleep I was rudely awoken by one of the others hearing scuttling animal sounds. So I put my earplugs in, and went to sleep.

Someone may have overfilled her cooking pot….

In a recent development, annabel eagerly checks what she has ‘rolled’. Photo by Sinéad.

The route briefing. Huts usually have helpful maps in them somewhere! Photo by Annabel.
